subject: Copywriting
title: Microtargeting and Filter Bubbles
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Microtargeting and Filter Bubbles.

hook.text: Cambridge Analytica used Facebook data from 87 million users to microtarget political ads during the 2016 election.

buildup.text: Microtargeting sends different messages to different people based on their psychology, fears, and interests.

discovery.text: Filter bubbles mean you only see information that confirms your existing beliefs.

twist.text: Cambridge Analytica went bankrupt after the scandal.

climax.text: When everyone receives personalized persuasion, shared reality dissolves.

punchline.text: 87 million profiles harvested. Personalized propaganda is now standard practice.

quiz.question: How many user profiles did Cambridge Analytica harvest?

details.summary: Microtargeting uses personal data to deliver tailored persuasion to individuals based on their psychology, demographics, and behavior. Combined with algorithmic filter bubbles that reinforce existing beliefs, it creates a propaganda environment where everyone sees a different version of reality.
details.whyItMatters: Microtargeting has fundamentally changed political and commercial persuasion. Understanding how personalized propaganda works helps people recognize when their information environment is being curated to manipulate them.
takeaways: Microtargeting delivers different messages to different people based on personal data
Filter bubbles reinforce existing beliefs and prevent exposure to opposing views
Cambridge Analytica demonstrated microtargeting's political power

faq.question: What data is used for microtargeting?
faq.answer: Everything from browsing history and purchase records to personality quiz results, social media activity, location data, and voter registration files. Cambridge Analytica famously used Facebook data to create psychological profiles for targeted political advertising.

faq.question: What is a filter bubble?
faq.answer: A filter bubble is the personalized information universe that algorithms create around each user. By showing content that matches existing preferences and beliefs, platforms inadvertently (or deliberately) isolate users from diverse perspectives, making them more susceptible to one-sided messaging.
